items.title: Andhra Pradesh CM Naidu plans to bring Investment Protection Act before state assembly Law will make land deals, factory permits, incentive promises l...
items.description_html:
Andhra Pradesh CM Naidu plans to bring Investment Protection Act before state assembly

Law will make land deals, factory permits, incentive promises legally locked so future governments cannot cancel them. This matters because AP foreign investment fell from $609m to $92m under previous regime that ran reverse tendering on every big project

Polavaram dam sat idle five years over political fights. India paid $305m settling Dabhol after Maharashtra cancelled one power deal post elections. No state tried fixing this through law, which makes no sense

Naidu’s proposed Investment Protection Act in Andhra Pradesh tackles one of India oldest investor problems. New state governments routinely cancel predecessor deals, and nobody questions this pattern. West Bengal threw out 30 years of industrial incentives under TMC.

Previous AP regime stopped Amaravati, pushed out Lulu Group, cancelled clean energy contracts worth billions. Goldman Sachs, SoftBank, Brookfield had money in AP and watched deals get reopened, which was careless

Centre tried similar protection law in 2020, dropped it without any follow up. AP is now doing what Centre refused to

Andhra Pradesh wants to pass Investment Protection Act that locks in deals for investors across political cycles But Indian law lets any state assembly change or remove acts made by previous assembly. Supreme Court in March 2026 said Maharashtra could change industrial policy even after 25 years.

So no future AP government is legally forced to keep this act. Investors still want it because visible political cost on reversal matters more than legal promise.

Right now cancelling deals costs nothing in Indian states, which is why so many do it

items.title: Interesting deal. Adyar Ananda Bhavan (A2B), a nearly 50 year old south Indian food chain, is being acquired by Bodhi Tree, which is run by James Murd...
items.description_html:
Interesting deal.

Adyar Ananda Bhavan (A2B), a nearly 50 year old south Indian food chain, is being acquired by Bodhi Tree, which is run by James Murdoch and JioStar vice chairman Uday Shankar.

Few points

- Bodhi Tree is taking majority stake for $180 million, which would peg valuation at $300-350 million (Rs 2,800-3,300 crore) based on back of the envelope math.

- Revenue was up 7% to Rs 1,500 crore, but net profit fell 8% to Rs 36 crore in FY25, as per Tracxn. That would imply a price to sales ration of around 2x.

This seems like a slight discount to listed fast food platforms like Devyani and Jubilant, which trade at 2.2-3x multiples. Interesting as A2B owns the brand, while Jubilant/Devyani run global franchises like Dominos, KFC.

- A2B has a network of 160 outlets in India and 30 overseas including Singapore, US and UK. Plan is to build it further globally, which would mean a push for packaged food biz expansion as well.

- In the past, majority stake deals of South Indian chains by PE firms like Adigas (NSR) and Sagar Ratna (India Equity Partners) have not worked out well, with legal battles with promoters.

Though with a seasoned operator like Uday Shankar becoming the board chair, I am guessing the transition from a promoter to professional management will be smoother.

- Investment also comes at a time when new chains like Benne Dosa and Rameshwaram Cafe are driving investor interest in the space.

items.title: US small businesses are signaling more inflation ahead: The proportion of US small firms planning to raise prices over the next 3 months rose +6 perce...
items.description_html:
US small businesses are signaling more inflation ahead:

The proportion of US small firms planning to raise prices over the next 3 months rose +6 percentage points in October, to 37%, the most since July 2022.

Excluding the post-pandemic surge in 2021 and 2022, this marks the highest reading since 2008.

By comparison, this figure did not exceed 30% between 2009 and 2019.

Furthermore, 33% of small firms raised prices over the last 3 months, the 3rd-highest reading since March 2023.

Meanwhile, 17% of business owners pointed to inflation as their single most important problem, up from 12% a year ago.

Small businesses are preparing for further price hikes as inflationary pressures mount.

This marks its 3rd consecutive monthly increase, up from +1.64% in July.

At the same time, core services less shelter inflation, also known as Supercore CPI and closely monitored by the Fed, rose to a 3-month annualized rate of +5.45%, its highest since mid-2024.

The weighted proportion of CPI components rising at an annualized rate above 2% soared to 76% last month, the largest percentage since August 2022.

This figure has risen +17 percentage points since July, marking its sharpest 3-month increase since early 2021.

The Fed's fight against inflation is far from over.

items.title: RT Amar Govindarajan: The Lodha Theoretical Physics Institute is quite different from any institute you may have heard about. The story behind its fou...
items.description_html:
RT Amar Govindarajan
The Lodha Theoretical Physics Institute is quite different from any institute you may have heard about.

The story behind its founding director’s career in theoretical physics is also quite unique.

What makes it different:
- Launched in Mumbai in May 2026 by the Lodha Foundation
-Theory only: no teaching, no grant-chasing, no admin, no degrees
-At public institutions, a professor can get “five minutes a day” for research, says Jain

Its founding director, Jainendra Jain, is a recipient of the Wolf Prize — in physics, it’s considered second only to the Nobel.

(Even after his physics PhD, his father kept mailing him UPSC forms so his son could become an IAS officer. Thankfully, Jain stuck to his guns.)

From Sambhar to Yale:
- Hindi-medium government school in a Rajasthan salt town
-Lost his mother and a foot in a tram accident at 12
-IIT Kanpur fees: ~Rs 35 a month, paid by a since-scrapped national scholarship

The puzzle he cracked:
-Squeeze electrons into an ultra-thin layer under a strong magnet, and their resistance moves in neat steps: 1, 2, 3
-Then came steps at odd fractions — 1/3, 2/5, 3/7 — that nobody could fully explain
-Jain’s idea, over Christmas 1988: each electron grabs a bit of the magnetic field and becomes a new particle, for which the fractions are whole numbers

A wonderful profile of Jainendra Jain and what the new institute is trying to do by @astrokaran (link in next tweet)

India has built a solar manufacturing base faster than any country outside China. What it now needs to do is to turn this capacity into competitive production across the value chain.

The report finds that India's dependence on imports has shifted upstream to cells and wafers. Cell imports rose to around US$3 billion in 2025-26, even as module imports declined.

India’s NBFC sector continues to expand, but the bigger story is the shift in where credit is flowing. NBFC Credit Grows 15.4% to Rs 61.7 Lakh Crore; Gold Loans Rise 66.1% in Sep 2026 highlights a clear move toward retail-led, asset-backed lending.

Key takeaways:
• NBFC credit grew 15.4% YoY to ₹61.7 lakh crore, with retail loans contributing nearly 59% of the incremental growth.
• Retail loan share increased to 43.5%, while industry’s share declined to 36.8%, indicating a continued portfolio rebalancing.
• Gold loans surged 66.1% YoY and accounted for 18% of incremental credit, despite representing only 6.1% of the NBFC loan book.
• Industry credit growth moderated to 7.4%, while banks continued to outpace NBFCs across most major segments except retail lending.

items.title: Our message to Nvidia's board: Do not fire Jensen Huang. There is no clear replacement for Jensen Huang. We are confident that his departure would ult...
items.description_html:
Our message to Nvidia's board:

Do not fire Jensen Huang.

There is no clear replacement for Jensen Huang. We are confident that his departure would ultimately be a net negative for Nvidia, its shareholders, and the AI Revolution.

First, take a look at the data. History also suggests that removing a successful CEO will come with a significant cost.

A study of 187 forced CEO departures from S&P 1500 companies found that removing outperforming CEOs resulted in negative long-term stock returns. This case would be no different, in our view.

Jensen Huang is the definition of an outperforming CEO. Nvidia's board must not make a decision in the heat of the moment.

The board should take the time to conduct a thorough investigation and consult with shareholders, with a strong emphasis on the latter.

Quite literally, Nvidia's board should convene a special shareholder meeting and hold an advisory vote on this decision. This is the most consequential CEO controversy in world history. Shareholders deserve a say.

In addition, Nvidia's stock, $NVDA, is now down -35% in 26 trading days, nearly half of which is a result of the recent scandal.

We believe Jensen Huang's potential removal as CEO is now ~80% priced in.

Why take an action with massive downside potential when the market has already priced in much of that risk?

The downside of retaining Huang may be limited, while the potential upside is tremendous.

Lastly, history shows that retaining Jensen Huang could still lead to a favorable outcome. In 2019, Amazon retained Jeff Bezos as CEO after his extramarital affair became public, and the company's stock subsequently surged +108% by 2021.

Personal misconduct should not be ignored, but it must also be distinguished from corporate wrongdoing and weighed against the consequences of removing an executive who is instrumental to the company's success.

We believe Jensen Huang is an irreplaceable part of Nvidia and the AI Revolution more broadly.

Once the dust settles, firing Jensen Huang would prove to be a costly mistake.

It is time to pause and consult your shareholders.

items.title: DGFT banned lithium-ion battery black mass exports on November 10, starting right away Black mass is powder made by shredding old batteries, containin...
items.description_html:
DGFT banned lithium-ion battery black mass exports on November 10, starting right away

Black mass is powder made by shredding old batteries, containing lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese But here is what makes this interesting, India exported zero black mass last fiscal year. Domestic refining companies like Attero, Rubamin, and Exigo already have more capacity than feedstock available

India has more refiners than waste to give them. This ban is preemptive, not reactive, and that is why it matters

Indonesia banned nickel ore exports to force local smelting. China restricted gallium, germanium, and rare earth shipments. India now bans battery black mass exports. Every big economy is keeping raw materials inside its borders for domestic processing.

I wrote up in my Copper Article Yu will connect the dots

Mineral supply chains are breaking apart faster than any trade deal can fix. India ban came days after launching ₹1,500 crore recycling scheme under its National Mineral Mission. 58 recyclers are already approved under it.

Banning exports without building domestic buyers creates wasted stockpiles, and India avoided that mistake by getting sequencing right

Banning black mass exports keeps lithium, cobalt, and nickel inside India But India has no cathode material factories at scale. Over 80% of recyclers shred batteries and stop at black mass. Few go further to extract usable metals.

Without cathode and anode production, recovered minerals sit with few domestic buyers. Commitments hit 850 kilotonnes against 270 kilotonne target, but refining beyond black mass barely exists.

But few Companies will do soon that too :) like HEG

https://www.normalguy.co.in/post/idealist-connecting-the-dot-3-oct-the-copper-supply-chain-chokepoint

items.title: US spent 3 years from 2022 to 2025 building rules to stop Nvidia chips reaching China December 2025, Trump allowed H200 chip sales at 25% cut going to...
items.description_html:
US spent 3 years from 2022 to 2025 building rules to stop Nvidia chips reaching China

December 2025, Trump allowed H200 chip sales at 25% cut going to Washington. Months later, Nvidia H200 chips pile up in Hong Kong warehouses because Beijing will not let them in. China may allow fewer than 200,000 foreign chips total. Nvidia booked $400 million in losses on chips nobody bought

Washington opened one door right when Beijing had closed its own. Security became commerce, and that commerce is not arriving

Huawei is making 600,000 Ascend 910C chips in 2026, double from last year. At same time, Nvidia H200s sit blocked in Hong Kong because Beijing will not approve them that matching number is not random, it is planned substitution

Beijing forces Chinese firms to buy Huawei by choking foreign supply. Quality gaps shrink under real demand pressure, then winners scale with state orders. Ascend chips are slower per unit but Beijing does not care about speed. It cares about owning supply. Once switched, buyers do not come back

China ran this same pattern in solar panels, EVs, and batteries. Let foreign tech in first. Subsidize domestic versions until they reach 70% of foreign quality. Make local firms fight each other on cost, Scale winners with state orders and cheap loans.

Then block imports once domestic makers fill demand. AI chips are now in that fighting phase. Huawei, Cambricon, and Biren compete while Beijing blocks Nvidia at customs.

Pattern is running right in front of everyone. Washington saw it in solar and still missed it here.

With 100 GW per year of cell production, SpaceX can power hundreds of thousands of satellites every year. All ground level debates about grid access and land for solar farms stop mattering when your buyer flies in orbit.

Musk is not fighting power companies. He is making computers that bring their own energy

SpaceX picked Singulus from Germany to make its HJT solar cell lines. Tesla separately ordered over $2 billion of equipment from Chinese makers. Same boss, split supply chain, and nobody in Washington saw this coming

items.title: India built 5 lakh circuit km of power lines by January 2026, Another 40,000 km are being built right now Old porcelain insulators break easily in dir...
items.description_html:
India built 5 lakh circuit km of power lines by January 2026, Another 40,000 km are being built right now

Old porcelain insulators break easily in dirty and salty air, and utilities kept using them anyway, wasting steel on every new line. Composite insulators are lighter, do not break from salt, and last longer. This market is growing at 6.7% every year toward $5 billion by 2035.

State power companies buy 42% of all composite insulators in India, and slow switching costs everyone. Cost savings here add up quickly

Porcelain insulators made Indian power companies build bigger, heavier towers with more steel and wider bases. Porcelain cracks in salty air, gets worse with pollution, and nobody fixed that for decades.

Composite insulators use silicone rubber and fiberglass instead. They weigh far less, so towers can be smaller and cheaper to build. For 400 kV and 765 kV power lines running through coastal and factory areas, porcelain was never built for those conditions.

Composite changes what utilities thought was normal. Better options exist right now

When you swap out one material in power lines, that change spreads across decades of new building. India grew its grid 71.6% since 2014, adding 209,000 circuit km, with 33 GW of HVDC power lines planned next.

Porcelain insulators need replacing every time dirty air or salt eats into them, and keeping them makes no sense. Composite polymer handles all of that and weighs 70% less.

Tower steel goes down, speed goes up, repair costs drop. One swap cuts 3 costs at once. Growing demand rewards early makers

items.title: RT Aditya Kalra: ‘NO SUCH ORDER PASSED BY HER LADYSHIP’ India’s government ordered blocking of 100+ illegal betting websites based on two court ord...
items.description_html:
RT Aditya Kalra
‘NO SUCH ORDER PASSED BY HER LADYSHIP’

India’s government ordered blocking of 100+ illegal betting websites based on two court orders. But @Reuters has found the court orders were fake.

The two court orders carried blue court seals, a fake QR code and made-up case numbers such as “Writ - A 30480/2026”. They were sent by individuals who claimed to be lawyers, and asked for immediate implementation by Indian government.

The government sent them to internet providers to take down websites. The forgeries are the latest sign that fake orders are slipping past India's official content removal mechanism, considered one of the world's strictest

Following questions from Reuters, Uttar Pradesh police have opened a forgery investigation after Reuters queries to the Allahabad High Court, while the Rajasthan High Court told Reuters in an email the order did not exist on its server.

Who sent the orders to the government & how did officials order takedowns? Read.

items.title: Good Example of How Real Estate Accounting Works! One of the most important things to understand about real estate companies is that pre-sales do not ...
items.description_html:
Good Example of How Real Estate Accounting Works!

One of the most important things to understand about real estate companies is that pre-sales do not immediately translate into reported REV & profits

Take Max Estates as an example!

In FY26, the company reported REV of just 199 Cr

However, 15,650 Cr of embedded REV & an estd 4,800-5,700 Cr of embedded PBT from sold units & launched projects, yet to be recognized in the P&L (Starting from FY28 onwards)

Under Ind AS 115, REV is recognized when the applicable conditions are met & control is transferred

This is why looking only at the current P&L is misleading for real estate developers

items.title: RT CSEINDIA: Delhi’s early-winter air pollution has worsened in 2026, with higher particulate levels than in previous years. A new analysis by the @C...
items.description_html:
RT CSEINDIA
Delhi’s early-winter air pollution has worsened in 2026, with higher particulate levels than in previous years.

A new analysis by the @CSEINDIA, released today, finds that emergency traffic curbs introduced by the government have not been enough to ease the pollution burden.

"Diwali pollution is an annual tipping point, but elevated particulate levels before the festival this year show that baseline pollution is higher than in previous years," says @AnumitaRoychowd, executive director, Research and Advocacy, CSE.

Among local sources, transport remains the largest contributor. While the share of stubble smoke rose during this period, severe pollution episodes continued even when farm fire contributions dropped.

"Delhi’s pre-winter pollution in 2026 was generally higher than in 2025, except for a brief late-September drop caused by rain. In both years, pollution surged in the days leading up to Diwali. However, the overall toxic burden during this pre-festive week was significantly worse in 2026 than in previous years," says @sharon_kour, deputy programme manager, Urban Lab, CSE.

Read the full analysis and press release: https://www.cseindia.org/cse-releases-early-winter-post-diwali-air-pollution-analysis-for-delhi-ncr-13335

items.title: AI is a six-layer investment opportunity. But which layer will capture the most profits and which will struggle to earn back its investment? That's th...
items.description_html:
AI is a six-layer investment opportunity. But which layer will capture the most profits and which will struggle to earn back its investment?

That's the question investors should be asking as billions flow into the AI ecosystem.

Because creating value from AI and capturing that value are two very different things.

Goldman Sachs maps the AI ecosystem into 6 interconnected layers:

Capital markets – Financing the AI revolution
Energy & data centers – Powering the infrastructure
Hardware & chips – Building the computing engine
Cloud infrastructure – Scaling AI globally
AI models & platforms – Turning compute into intelligence
Applications & customers – Monetizing AI adoption

Each layer has different economics, capital intensity, competitive dynamics, and profit potential.

Here's the investment paradox:

The companies spending the most on AI infrastructure may not be the companies earning the highest returns.

Some layers could benefit from pricing power and structural bottlenecks.

Others could face commoditization, margin pressure, and intense competition.

And the most exciting businesses may not necessarily be the most attractive investments at today's valuations.

The real opportunity lies in identifying which of these six layers will capture a disproportionate share of AI's future profits before the market fully prices it in.

items.description_html:
RT ValueEquity
Absolutely must watch , there is always a point in research where once you know enough about the company /sector , there is no point knowing , because to make an investable decision there is only so much you need to know

Lot of investors try to understand every single moving part , try to predict complex adaptive systems , forecasting to the decimal on what happens , when the real thing to do is to be aware that things you cannot control you will never be able to control

Am I taking over the business from the management as a promoter = NO

Am I participating as a shareholder= yes

where trusting the management to do better job than my Air conditioned desk hypocrisy to tell the guy on the shop floor what is better is not my role /capabilty

My role is to trust the management on the levers that I cannot understand /control , and that is where qualitiatives matter more than quantitatives in many cases and then make my thesis

Only that amount of research that helps you make the investable decision is important , because after a point more research can be counter productive and dilutive of clear decision making

My opinion , hence it comes to the same analogy , how to make the better decisions on the back of incomplete information but still keep the odds high to someone who lives in the illusion of forecasting, that is the true qualitative factor

Again , just my opinion in full agreement to Stan Druckenmiller


Ted Zhang: Stan Druckenmiller: Knowing When to Stop Analyzing Is the Biggest Mistake We Make

Absolutely must watch , there is always a point in research where once you know enough about the company /sector , there is no point knowing , because to make an investable decision there is only so much you need to know

Lot of investors try to understand every single moving part , try to predict complex adaptive systems , forecasting to the decimal on what happens , when the real thing to do is to be aware that things you cannot control you will never be able to control

Am I taking over the business from the management as a promoter = NO

Am I participating as a shareholder= yes

where trusting the management to do better job than my Air conditioned desk hypocrisy to tell the guy on the shop floor what is better is not my role /capabilty

My role is to trust the management on the levers that I cannot understand /control , and that is where qualitiatives matter more than quantitatives in many cases and then make my thesis

Only that amount of research that helps you make the investable decision is important , because after a point more research can be counter productive and dilutive of clear decision making

My opinion , hence it comes to the same analogy , how to make the better decisions on the back of incomplete information but still keep the odds high to someone who lives in the illusion of forecasting, that is the true qualitative factor

Again , just my opinion in full agreement to Stan Druckenmiller


Ted Zhang: Stan Druckenmiller: Knowing When to Stop Analyzing Is the Biggest Mistake We Make

I think it's the biggest mistake in our business. At some point, the analysis becomes counterproductive. That's one thing I've learned, and it's greatly to my advantage. Speed matters now. With AI

items.description_html:
One of the activities which I have included in my schedule is to watch management interviews before ending the day.

Why so?

Management gets to talk a lot about the business prospects and sometimes you get more information vs a standard concall where book keeping questions sometimes give information which isn't useful.

For eg:- Along with reading concall of one Power equipment co. I always watched their management interviews post earnings season. The plans they laid out post IPO about their expansion in these interviews were extremely crisp and easy to understand. The PAT of the co has now gone from 100 crores to more than 220 in last 2 years. Every interview gives a hint on how not just the growth but the capabilities of the co will be bigger in next 2 years.

Another example is that of a defence co promoter who kept misguiding in these interviews about tall targets. These interviews really give you an idea about how the management communicates with the street and the retail investor+Whether they walk the talk or not.

@stockscansin we have made sure that all such important interviews are available under interview scans!

items.title: In forging, you can make more money by shipping less metal. A 30 kg black forging at ₹130/kg bills ₹3,900. Machine it down to 20 kg, sell it at ₹30...
items.description_html:
In forging, you can make more money by shipping less metal.

A 30 kg black forging at ₹130/kg bills ₹3,900. Machine it down to 20 kg, sell it at ₹300/kg, and the same part bills ₹6,000.

A third lighter, 54% more revenue. It’s like cutting a diamond: you lose weight, but every carat that’s left is worth far more.

As a forger climbs from black forgings to heat-treated parts, precision CNC components, sub-assemblies and finally aero, defence and EV systems, indicative realisations rise from ₹110–140/kg to ₹800–2,500/kg, and operating margins go from 8–12% to 20–30%+.

Why?

At the bottom, most of the price is steel passed straight through to the customer. Higher up, the customer pays for precision, engineering and a ready-to-fit part, and steel becomes a far smaller slice of the bill.

items.description_html:
RT Nigel D'Souza
India has gone from last to first.
Source: Emkay note

Over the past four weeks, Indian equities have surged 13.9% in dollar terms, making India the best performer among 11 major markets over 1, 3 & 6 months. Three weeks ago, it ranked last on 3-month returns.

But this is catch-up, not yet leadership. India has recovered roughly 40% of its relative underperformance versus emerging markets over the past year.

Trends that stand out:
Decoupling: India's correlation with global markets has fallen close to zero, a 10-year low. Domestic factors are driving markets for now.
Asian tech weakness: Taiwan (-22%) & Korea (-24%) are down sharply over four weeks.
Capital rotation: Money flowing out of Asian tech is improving India's relative standing.

Will India sustain this outperformance?

items.description_html:
RT Capitalmind
In July 2001, 2 crore Indians found out they couldn't get their money out of India's most trusted investment.

US-64 paid tax-free dividends for years at a price UTI simply announced. No NAV, holdings carried at cost, and dividends paid out of reserves until the reserves went negative.

Then the 2001 crash hit, redemptions poured in, and UTI froze repurchases. The government bailout cost around Rs 14,000 crore.

Almost every rule fund houses follow today (publish the NAV, disclose holdings, no guaranteed returns) traces back to this.

In this episode of the Capitalmind Podcast, @deepakshenoy and @shraychandra discuss what went wrong with US-64, and what it changed for the Mutual Fund industry

items.title: RT Christophe Barraud 🇫🇷 🇲🇨: 🇨🇳 China's exports surged 35.2% YoY in October with high-tech exports up 66.6% and integrated circuits ...
items.description_html:
RT Christophe Barraud 🇫🇷 🇲🇨
🇨🇳 China's exports surged 35.2% YoY in October with high-tech exports up 66.6% and integrated circuits jumping 137.1%. Impressive numbers but a rather worrying economic paradox lies.

📊 High-tech products now account for nearly 34% of China's total exports and explain roughly 52% of their annual increase in value. China is benefiting massively from the global technology investment cycle and specifically in AI. However, Chinese exports of integrated circuits increased by 111.1% in value over the first ten months of the year but by only 3.2% in volume. This divergence reflects an increase in the average value of exported components rather than a comparable surge in the quantities shipped.

📈 Another interesting figure is the 41.6% increase in imports. Some might interpret this as evidence of a real recovery in Chinese consumption but a significant share of these imports is used to supply China's manufacturing sector, especially its technology supply chains. Importing more components to manufacture equipment that will be exported doesn't mean domestic demand is recovering. Domestic consumption remains insufficient to sustain growth on its own and China's cumulative trade surplus has already exceeded $1 trillion over the first ten months of the year, highlighting just how dependent the country remains on foreign demand.

⚠️ This situation could become problematic in 2027. The more China benefits from global AI investment, the more certain segments of its industrial economy become dependent on that spending continuing. If hyperscalers begin slowing their capital expenditure because returns fail to justify the investments, the consequences could spread throughout the entire industrial supply chain, from electronic components to computing equipment. Add to that increasingly demanding base effects and the possibility of escalating trade tensions with the US and Europe. China is becoming simultaneously more powerful industrially and potentially more vulnerable to economic decisions made abroad.

The more China strengthens its global manufacturing dominance, the more its economic growth risks becoming dependent on external demand that it cannot fully control.

items.title: "Indian industry does not support." ​Sterling and Wilson’s latest concall exposes the ground-level pain in India’s Solar EPC space right now: 1. Gr...
items.description_html:
"Indian industry does not support."

Sterling and Wilson’s latest concall exposes the ground-level pain in India’s Solar EPC space right now:

1. Grid & PPA Bottlenecks: Unsigned PPAs and heavy grid curtailment across Rajasthan & Gujarat have brought domestic order inflows from IPPs and PSUs to a crawl.

2. Policy Mismatch: BESS mandates require domestic sourcing, but India lacks the manufacturing base. The result? Irrational quotes, cancelled orders, and contractors failing to execute.

3. Revenue Risk: Growth is heavily backloaded to Q4, relying almost entirely on international projects to hit a modest 10% guidance.
A sector with massive paper pipeline, but severe execution reality checks.

A sector with massive paper pipeline, but severe execution reality checks.

RT Neil Thomas 牛犇
Excited to start today as the Senior Geoeconomics Analyst for China at @Bloomberg

Friday was my last day full-time at @AsiaSociety . I am incredibly proud to have contributed to the success of the Center for China Analysis in the past few years as it has grown to become a leading think tank on Chinese politics, economy, foreign policy, and more.

Deeply grateful to my boss Jing Qian for his leadership and friendship, to our leader @MrKRudd for his vision and drive, to my CCA colleagues Betty Wang, Jamie Lui, Jennifer Choo, @Kate_K_Logan , Kevin Zongzhe Li, @wstv_lizzi , @LyleJMorris , @LiShuo_GP , @Taylahbland , and Wenxuan Ma for their dedication and expertise; and to the entire CCA, @AsiaPolicy , and Asia Society communities.

I am especially indebted to my incredible colleagues past and present in the politics program — Lobsang Tsering, @shuizaiping2 , @harrisonwang2 , Alex Fan, @yifanz0303 , @HungChingFei , Yuxuan Wei, @tl__03 , @LiZhuoran0322 , and David Zhong — for their hard work and intellectual companionship. They will continue to make outstanding contributions.

But this is not goodbye! I will remain part of the CCA family as a non-resident honorary senior fellow, complete some exciting grant projects, and contribute however I can to the center’s continued success.

Looking forward to CCA reaching new heights in the years ahead!

Re @archgen_ is building skyscrapers for semiconductor chips

Shrinking transistors is getting harder. Stacking them makes heat harder to manage. We’re building the tools to design chips in three dimensions.

We stack transistors vertically, shorten connections, and optimize timing and heat together.

Our foundational model for thermal simulation, predicts temperature roughly 5,000× faster than conventional EDA tools.

Our placement engine ranked #1 in HRT’s macro-placement challenge

We’re working with some of the largest fabs in the world to tape out our first chip in April 2027

RT Richard Turrin
1/6🧵 #DEDOLLARIZATION DAILY:

Yuan internationalization is as JPM Asset Management puts it: “steady, slow, but nonstop.”

But leave it to Andy Mukherjee (@andymukherjee70) to reveal what most Western analysts miss: it’s not just Beijing pushing the yuan into the world. It’s Goldman, JPMorgan, and BofA lining up for Chinese capital.

Wall Street banks have raised 134 billion yuan in offshore bonds in Hong Kong this year, nearly triple all of 2025.

For the first time ever, Hong Kong is on track to arrange more bond sales in yuan than in dollars.

The same banks Washington expects to enforce dollar dominance are quietly building the plumbing for its competitor.

Each article in this thread shows a different rail. Bonds. Gold. Payments. Digital infrastructure.

None of them alone is a tidal wave. Together they’re reshaping the map.

Indium Phosphide (InP) substrates require ultra-high-purity raw materials, precision crystal growth, high-pressure processing, and advanced wafer polishing.

What makes this interesting? The real technological moat may lie in the crystal-growth equipment, process know-how, and ability to achieve consistent wafer quality at scale.

A critical part of the compound semiconductor supply chain worth understanding.

India's banking sector continues to report stronger asset quality metrics, with the Net NPA ratio touching a historic low of 0.34% in Q2FY27. But as the legacy NPA clean-up nears completion, the focus is shifting from resolution to managing emerging pockets of risk.

Key takeaways from our latest BFSI Research note:
• Gross NPA ratio declined to 1.54%, while Net NPA ratio reached a record low of 0.34%.
• Fresh slippages fell 13.3% QoQ, with recoveries and upgrades covering 68% of fresh stress.
• Provision coverage improved to 78.1%, strengthening loss-absorption buffers.
• Restructured loan books continued to shrink across both PSBs and PVBs.
• The key watchpoint remains the agriculture portfolio, where a weak monsoon could drive higher stress levels in FY28.

items.description_html:
Is West Bengal finally seeing an industrial turnaround? Some very interesting developments!

Reliance: Exploring a massive ₹2 lakh crore nuclear power project at Haripur. Could be a landmark investment for Bengal.

Ashok Leyland: Remember Singur, where Tata's Nano plant never took off? The company is now in preliminary talks with the government for a heavy vehicle manufacturing facility there!

Vedanta: Exploring ₹70,000–80,000 crore investment in aluminium and power near Asansol, where it already owns land.

JSW Group: Around ₹50,000 crore of investment plans across power and other sectors. Bhoomi pujan for its second thermal power unit is expected in January 2027.
These are big numbers, but most projects are still at the proposal or discussion stage.

Bengal was once among India's biggest industrial hubs. Would be wonderful to see it regain that position!

The real turnaround will be when announcements translate into factories, production and jobs.

Everyone openly talks about the North South divide ,the division is in the East West section

The government just introduced the new industrial policy yesterday

Definitely a state worth tracking closely!

items.title: India does not produce any potash at all and nobody in government seems bothered by this Every gram comes from other countries. Fertiliser subsidy was...
items.description_html:
India does not produce any potash at all and nobody in government seems bothered by this

Every gram comes from other countries. Fertiliser subsidy was ₹1.88 lakh crore last year and could nearly double to ₹3.42 lakh crore by FY27. Government gave ₹1.27 lakh crore for making computer chips in India. Rare earths got ₹7,300 crore for special magnet factories But potash, which goes into food production for 1.46 billion people, got nothing.

It is on government own strategic minerals list since 2023, yet nothing moved

India mines zero potash and buys all of it from abroad, yet nobody treats this as dangerous. 40% comes from Canada, but relations between both countries turned sour and imports dropped 13% last year.

Russia sends another big portion but faces global sanctions pressure. Every shipment passes through narrow sea routes like Strait of Hormuz and Suez Canal, routes that saw disruption in recent conflicts. India keeps only 30 to 45 days of fertiliser reserves.

If ships get stuck during planting season, farmers lose potash supply before government can respond

Rajasthan has 89% of India total potash deposits, around 23,091 million tonnes. Punjab found more deposits in Fazilka district recently. India even has 2 billion tonnes of glauconite, which is another source of potash But nobody is mining any of it, which is hard to justify.

Potash is not included under rules that allow private companies to bid for mining rights. Government keeps forming committees and making plans but digging has not started.

India pays $1.3 billion every year to import potash while refusing to touch its own reserves

items.title: Guyana said it can send India 1 million barrels of oil every day Guyana makes around 900,000 barrels of oil per day right now from 4 offshore platform...
items.description_html:
Guyana said it can send India 1 million barrels of oil every day

Guyana makes around 900,000 barrels of oil per day right now from 4 offshore platforms. But it offered India 1 million barrels daily, more than what it produces today that offer is based on future production, not current supply. Guyana hopes to reach 1.9 million barrels per day by 2030 with 3 more projects coming.

India needs 5.5 million barrels every day and cannot wait until 2029 for supply to show up. Russia and Gulf together still supply 78% of India crude and that will not change soon

Indian refineries are designed for heavy, sour crude oil from Gulf and Russia. Guyana produces light, sweet oil called Liza grade, which is very different. Changing refineries to handle sweet crude costs billions and takes years.

India bought 2 million trial barrels from Guyana in 2021 and never ordered again because refinery match was poor. Guyana is also offering refinery and bunkering partnerships but India’s 23 refineries cannot change their crude diet quickly.

Guyana is shopping for buyers because European demand dropped and Liza crude got cheaper

items.title: RT Jukan: Taiwanese semiconductor analyst Andrew Lu’s take on the recent scandal involving Jensen Huang: Why the US Seized on the Scandal to Draw Its...
items.description_html:
RT Jukan
Taiwanese semiconductor analyst Andrew Lu’s take on the recent scandal involving Jensen Huang:

Why the US Seized on the Scandal to Draw Its Sword: Three Strategic Objectives

The purpose of this scandal is by no means to expose an affair. It is to force through three critical objectives that had made no headway in the tech war between the US and China because Jensen Huang opposed them.

The first cut: Completely destroy the legitimacy of Jensen Huang's lobbying against sanctions in Washington

Over the past two years, the loudest and most influential business leader in Silicon Valley opposing a total ban on chip exports to China has been Jensen Huang. He has told the White House the same thing all along: "Cede the Chinese market to Huawei, and the only one that ends up dead is the American tech industry."

But the moment US intelligence labels the woman named as Huang's affair partner "a spy working for China's Ministry of State Security who sought to steer the US toward easing its chip controls," every bit of lobbying he has done for looser controls takes on an entirely different political meaning. It becomes a national security matter, raising the possibility that a foreign spy used a secret relationship to exert influence.

Huang can no longer say a single word in defense of the Chinese market before Congress or the White House. If he does, he will be branded as someone who "fell for an intelligence operation and still hasn't come to his senses."

The second cut: Reverse the H200 export approvals for China and sever the link between Chinese shell companies and Southeast Asian smuggling networks

Look at the timing of the two reports.

On November 8, the very day the Jensen Huang scandal broke, The New York Times published an investigation for which its reporters went in person to dozens of Chinese companies that the US Commerce Department had approved to handle Nvidia's H200 chips. New Matrix in Beijing was one of them. According to the report, the registered addresses of companies approved to buy the chips turned out to be empty "ghost offices," and some of the companies had close ties to entities on US sanctions lists and to firms under contract with the Chinese military.

One exposé says Nvidia's CEO was having an affair with a female spy from Megaspeed, the Singapore company that handled the chip smuggling. The other says the Chinese companies Commerce approved to buy H200s are nothing but shell companies trading on behalf of the Chinese military. The aim of these two reports is clear. They are meant to pressure the Trump administration and the Commerce Department into fully revoking or freezing H200 export approvals for China and, going further, to force a sweeping overhaul of the loophole that let chips be diverted through data centers run by third parties in Singapore and elsewhere in Southeast Asia.

The third cut: Put Nvidia on a national security leash through congressional oversight and an independent investigation

As the world's largest company by market cap and the dominant force in AI, Nvidia has until now enjoyed broad autonomy in how it runs its business. But in the wake of this incident, the three congressional committees responsible for China, foreign affairs, and intelligence have begun examining Nvidia's internal security measures directly. They have even pressured Nvidia's board into forming an independent investigation committee to look into the company's own founder and CEO.

In effect, Washington's national security establishment has planted a watchdog right inside Nvidia's board. From now on, the goal is to make sure that everything, down to where each and every one of Nvidia's high performance chips ends up, conforms strictly to US national security strategy. It also means there is no more room for skirting the edge of the rules or releasing chips with specs specially tailored to regulatory thresholds.

Conclusion

"The scandal was a detonator set off right on cue. The real goal was to plug the holes chips were leaking through."

Jensen Huang made the fatal mistake of letting his guard down in his private life and personal relationships. In the end, he fell into a honey trap, the textbook tactic of intelligence warfare, and was compromised. America's national security and intelligence agencies ruthlessly exploited the weakness his private life had exposed. As a result, they solved three thorny problems in a single stroke: Nvidia's lobbying at the White House to ease restrictions on China, the flow of H200 chips into Chinese shell companies, and smuggling routed through Singapore.

The closed congressional hearing set for November 18 will be the decisive turning point at which the US moves in earnest to tighten its sanctions on China's AI compute even further.

items.title: I’ve just finished reading William Hogeland’s book on Hamilton. As a hard-core admirer of Hamilton since the early 1990s, and someone who has long r...
items.description_html:
I’ve just finished reading William Hogeland’s book on Hamilton.

As a hard-core admirer of Hamilton since the early 1990s, and someone who has long regarded him as the greatest of the Founding Fathers, I think it is a brilliant book, even though Hogeland sets out quite deliberately to demolish Hamilton’s highly romanticized current reputation. He shows that Hamilton’s ambitions were not particularly democratic, although I suspect many of us already knew that, and had long thought that, for all his genius, or perhaps precisely because of it, he would have made a dangerous president who would have undermined democratic institutions. Nonetheless, the book confirms, even more than many of the more favorable accounts, just how brilliant, far-seeing, and hard-working a figure he was.

In a way, it is also a very good explanation of why democracy is simultaneously so grubby and yet the best of all political systems. It is built around institutional adjustment, a system that may seem messy but that. effectively prevents any one individual or group from taking the country too far in any direction.

Democracy may not be especially efficient in the short term, but it is incredibly efficient in the long term. Even a genius like Hamilton, with his extraordinary gifts, ferocious energy, powerful allies, and formidable reputation, could not take the country too far down a dangerous road. Other countries could learn from that.

The book has also greatly increased my interest in Albert Gallatin, the great opponent of Hamilton, whose statue in front of the US Treasury I have always resented. In Hogeland’s telling, he turns out to have been a great builder and rather like Hamilton himself.

P.S. Interesting trivia. It seems that the body of Charles Atlas was the model for both Hamilton's statue and Gallatin's statue.

items.title: Aptus Value Housing : Asset quality concerns continue❗️ Q2FY27 AUM 🔼20% - 14,177 Cr PAT 🔼18% - 267 Cr RoA - 7.7% | RoE - 20.1% Profitability h...
items.description_html:
Aptus Value Housing : Asset quality concerns continue❗️

Q2FY27
AUM 🔼20% - 14,177 Cr
PAT 🔼18% - 267 Cr
RoA - 7.7% | RoE - 20.1%

Profitability has never been the major concern for Aptus

The real disappointment has been execution against management's own guidance

At the beginning of FY26, management had guided for 24-25% disbursement growth & 28-30% AUM growth

However, FY26 eventually ended with just 11% disbursement growth & 21% AUM growth

Management repeatedly revised its growth expectations throughout the year, citing seasonality, competitive pressures, exit from smaller ticket loans & operational disruptions

Coming to asset quality, this has been another recurring concern across multiple concalls!

GNPA increased from 1.19% in Mar'25 to 1.68% in Sep'26 & 30+ DPD deteriorated from 5.91% to 7.08%

Management has repeatedly attributed these pressures to seasonality, collection delays & stress in the NBFC portfolio

The important distinction is that the core Housing Finance business remains healthy, with GNPA at 1.48% & H1 credit costs of just 25 bps

However, the NBFC business continues to face challenges, with GNPA at 2.17% & credit costs of 169 bps

Management has now revised its FY27 consolidated credit cost guidance upwards by another 5-10 bps

Analysts have repeatedly questioned why asset quality has not improved meaningfully despite the company exiting smaller ticket loans & strengthening its collection infrastructure

On the growth front, management continues to maintain its FY27 AUM growth target of 22%, despite indicating that growth could moderate during Q3 because of tighter NBFC underwriting

It expects a recovery in Q4, supported by the contribution from newly opened branches & improving sourcing channels

Management needs to demonstrate consistent growth delivery & sustained improvement in NBFC asset quality

The business remains fundamentally profitable, but rebuilding investor confidence will require consistent execution!

items.title: Sometimes stocks can de-rate without any reason or just because of lack of market interest. One eg recently is that of Time technoplast where the co h...
items.description_html:
Sometimes stocks can de-rate without any reason or just because of lack of market interest.

One eg recently is that of Time technoplast where the co has consistently delivered 20%+ PAT growth, deleveraged and the volumes have grown in double digits.

Yet, the PE multiple has de-rated from 30x to 15x and stock has effectively gone through a time correction of 2 years. In the most recent Quarter as well they have delivered nearly 25%+ PAT growth.

The more one spends time in markets, the more one gets to learn about different situations. Time correction or just lack of interest is something that can happen in smallcaps.

Disc: no reco to buy or sell. Pure idea is to share the mental model of time corrections in small caps.

While growth remains broadly resilient, inflationary pressures, energy market volatility and diverging fiscal trajectories continue to influence sovereign and economic prospects worldwide.

𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬:

• Escalating tensions in West Asia continue to pose risks to global energy markets and inflation dynamics.
• AI-enabling goods are emerging as a powerful driver of global trade, with Asia at the forefront of this shift.

Evidence from Southern Europe suggests they can.

CareEdge Global IFSC Limited’s latest sovereign insight examines how digital tax-administration tools such as e-invoicing, real-time transaction reporting, and data-driven compliance monitoring are helping countries narrow VAT gaps and strengthen revenue collection.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀:

• Digital tax administration is helping governments boost revenue without increasing tax rates, making it an increasingly attractive policy tool amid rising fiscal pressures.
• Southern Europe offers a compelling success story. Greece, Italy, Portugal and Cyprus have significantly narrowed VAT compliance gaps through e-invoicing, real-time transaction reporting and data-driven tax enforcement.
• The results have been tangible: Greece's VAT gap fell from around 25% to 9% between 2018 and 2024, while Italy and Portugal also recorded sizeable improvements alongside stronger VAT revenues.
• Technology alone was not enough. The strongest outcomes occurred where digital tools were combined with stronger tax institutions, risk-based audits and measures that encouraged voluntary compliance.
• The benefits extend beyond public finances. Greater tax compliance supports economic formalisation, improves competition and enhances firms' access to finance and investment opportunities.
• As governments seek to strengthen fiscal buffers, improving tax compliance may offer one of the few remaining avenues to raise revenue while supporting long-term productivity and growth.

items.title: A day late in catching up on a very interesting report by @pranjulb on two changes coming to India’s current account balance and hence possibly the r...
items.description_html:
A day late in catching up on a very interesting report by @pranjulb on two changes coming to India’s current account balance and hence possibly the rupee.

➡️ First, India’s data centre build out will likely widen the CAD initially as imports for the build out of these facilities rise. Chips / cooling infrastructure etc will all add to imports.

- While this CAD negative, it need not be rupee negative if: 1) the build out is financed by ECBs/FDI), 2) If it is a staggered build-out.

➡️ A second CAD change could come from the spate of FTAs India is signing. In the past trade agreements have widened India’s trade deficit. But the report says that if initial imports are more capital goods, they could be medium-term positive.

-One way to make these agreements “rupee friendly”, the report says, is to pursue FDI alongside.

Lots to think about! But great read, Pranjul!

CareEdge Ratings' latest analysis suggests the relief in bank funding costs was driven more by liquidity conditions than structural repricing. As surplus liquidity has rapidly drained and policy tightening resumes, the road ahead may look different.

Key takeaways:

• Fresh bank spreads narrowed 4 bps m-o-m to 2.90%,as lending rates fell faster than deposit rates.
• Fresh deposit rates fell to 5.61%, the lowest in 10 months, aided by FCNR(B)-driven liquidity surplus.
• Banks are paying 94 bps less on fresh deposits than their existing deposit book, creating near-term support for margins as deposits reprice lower.
• Credit growth at 19.4% y-o-y continues to outpace deposit growth, while liquidity surplus has declined sharply, indicating a changing funding environment.
• CareEdge expects fresh spreads to widen modestly in October, with pressure likely shifting to the March quarter as deposit repricing catches up.

CareEdge Ratings’ latest analysis highlights that non-food bank credit growth remained robust at 19.1% y-o-y in September 2026, with momentum strengthening across all major sectors.

Key takeaways:
• Services credit led the pack, growing 28.3%, driven largely by bank lending to NBFCs, which surged 41.8% y-o-y.
• Industry credit expanded 19.5%, with MSMEs outpacing large industries, although large borrowers still accounted for the majority of incremental credit.
• Personal loans grew 17.3%, supported by housing, vehicle financing, and continued strength in gold-backed lending.
• Infrastructure credit improved to 11.8%, with the power sector driving most of the expansion.
• CareEdge expects credit growth to moderate to 15%-16% by FY27-end as base effects strengthen and gold loan growth normalises.

Nepal's macroeconomic profile remains resilient, but emerging risks warrant close attention. Our latest Nepal Economy Update - September 2026 highlights a delicate balance between external sector strength and inflationary pressures.

Key takeaways:
• CPI inflation accelerated to 6.3%, rising above the central bank's FY27 target, driven by higher food and transportation costs.
• Robust remittance inflows (+23.9% y-o-y) supported a stronger current account surplus, BoP surplus, and foreign exchange reserves of USD 26.5 billion.
• Merchandise exports surged 61.9% y-o-y, but a widening trade deficit underscores continued dependence on imports, particularly petroleum products.
• Tourism recovery remains intact, with arrivals continuing to move closer to pre-pandemic levels despite climatic disruptions.

items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
🚨 MORGAN STANLEY JUST FLAGGED A $250 BILLION AI RISK HIDING IN THE SOFTWARE CREDIT MARKET.

While Nomura and Bernstein highlight the enormous opportunity in AI infrastructure, Morgan Stanley reveals the other side of the boom.

And the numbers are alarming.

Morgan Stanley analyzed ~$250B of software loans:

🔴 16% HIGH AI disruption risk (~$40B)
🟡 49% Moderate risk
🟢 35% Low risk

But here's where it gets interesting:

• ~$20B of high-risk software loans already trade at distressed levels.

• Average loan prices: 97 for low-risk vs. 73 for high-risk borrowers.

• ~75% of high-risk exposure matures during 2027–2029.

• Weaker borrowers could face 550–1,000 bps in additional refinancing costs.

• Front-office applications have the highest share of high-risk loans at 32%.

These are AI vulnerability assessments, not default forecasts.

NOW CONNECT THE THREE REPORTS:

NOMURA: AI data centers are already generating substantial operating profits. Negative FCF largely reflects heavy upfront investment.

BERNSTEIN: OpenAI's infrastructure commitments may be more manageable than feared, but compute oversupply could pressure neocloud economics.

MORGAN STANLEY: AI disruption risk is already influencing software debt valuations—and refinancing pressure could intensify before earnings fully reflect disruption.

THE BIGGER PICTURE:

AI is creating extraordinary opportunities in infrastructure while threatening the economics of weaker software businesses.

The next big AI trade may not just be about who captures the billions flowing INTO AI infrastructure.

It may be about who loses pricing power, who struggles to refinance, and who gets left holding the debt.

AI isn't just reshaping technology.

It's starting to reshape credit markets.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: 🚨 OPEC: The real oil price shock isn't just crude. It's the cost of moving it. Shipping crude oil from the Middle Ea...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
🚨 OPEC: The real oil price shock isn't just crude. It's the cost of moving it.

Shipping crude oil from the Middle East to East Asia has become dramatically more expensive in just 9 months.

OPEC's November 2026 data reveals a staggering escalation in tanker freight and insurance costs.

📊 The numbers are alarming:

VLCC freight costs:

• January 2026: $3.18/barrel
• October 2026: $37.13/barrel

🔺 Nearly 12x higher

Marine insurance costs:

• January 2026: $0.06/barrel
• October 2026: $12.29/barrel

🔺 More than 200x higher

Combined freight + insurance:

• January: $3.24/barrel
• October: $49.42/barrel

That's an additional $46.18 per barrel in transportation and insurance costs.

⚠️ Freight and insurance now account for 30% of total crude oil costs on this route, compared with just 5% in January.

A sixfold increase in their share of total costs.
OPEC also highlights a critical point:

Current disruptions to the tanker fleet explain only a small fraction of the surge in shipping costs and insurance premiums.

These elevated costs are being transmitted through the value chain, increasing expenses for oil producers and consumers while adding inflationary pressure to the global economy.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: 🚨 BERNSTEIN JUST DROPPED A MAJOR REPORT ON THE $750 BILLION AI INFRASTRUCTURE BOOM. After Nomura argued that AI data...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
🚨 BERNSTEIN JUST DROPPED A MAJOR REPORT ON THE $750 BILLION AI INFRASTRUCTURE BOOM.

After Nomura argued that AI data centers are far more profitable than investors think, Bernstein tackles an even bigger question:

Can OpenAI actually afford its massive compute commitments and who ultimately captures the profits?

The findings are fascinating:

• $750B vs. $614B: Bernstein models ~$614B in OpenAI infrastructure payments through 2030, with annual spending potentially peaking at $184B in 2031. Not every announced commitment is binding, and actual spending could be lower.

• OpenAI's revenue is catching up: Bernstein cites a ~$50B annualized revenue run rate in September 2026, growing ~77% YoY. If growth remains strong, revenue could scale faster than infrastructure obligations.

• Oracle's $300B opportunity: Capacity comes online in stages, with Bernstein estimating only ~57% of modeled OpenAI contract revenue recognized through Oracle FY2030. The backlog represents a multiyear revenue opportunity, not immediate cash generation.

• Microsoft and Amazon have structural advantages: Their integrated cloud platforms, enterprise ecosystems and AI services offer more durable economics than simply renting GPUs.

• CoreWeave faces a different challenge: Bernstein is comfortable with existing contracts but questions renewal economics once compute becomes less scarce.

• The biggest risk may be oversupply, not OpenAI defaulting. Bernstein sees potential supply-demand normalization within 2–3 years, putting pressure on GPU rental prices and weaker infrastructure providers.

HERE'S THE REAL INSIGHT:

Nomura explains why AI infrastructure can remain profitable despite negative free cash flow.

Bernstein explains why that profitability won't necessarily be distributed equally.

The first phase of the AI boom rewarded companies that could secure GPUs, power and data-center capacity.

The next phase may reward companies that control customers, platforms and pricing power.

AI demand can keep exploding while returns on undifferentiated compute infrastructure deteriorate.

Being bullish on AI infrastructure spending is NOT the same as being bullish on every AI infrastructure stock.

That distinction could define the next leg of the AI trade.

items.description_html:
Lower Valuations Today Could Drive FII Inflows Tomorrow

An interesting study by JM Financial suggests that FII flows follow valuations with a 4–5 month lag.

Historical data from 2006–2026 reveals:

• Below 15x P/E: Average FII inflows of $18.8 billion over the next 12 months.
• 15–18x P/E: Average inflows of $14.1 billion.
• 18–21x P/E: Average inflows of $11 billion.
• Above 21x P/E: Average outflows of $4.3–4.7 billion.

Where Are We Today?
The Nifty trades at ~17.1x one-year forward P/E, placing it in a historically favourable valuation zone for FII inflows.

items.title: RT Nimesh Shah: UBS on SBI Neutral, TP Rs 1100 Reported a mixed quarter with strong NII growth of 5% QoQ and NIM of 2.94% (+8bp), both ahead of est. Y...
items.description_html:
RT Nimesh Shah
UBS on SBI
Neutral, TP Rs 1100
Reported a mixed quarter with strong NII growth of 5% QoQ and NIM of 2.94% (+8bp), both ahead of est.
Yet, loan growth of 18.2% YoY (19% in 1Q) & 3% miss on PPOP due to higher opex were key negatives
There was also a one-time gain from SBI MF listing of Rs72.9bn but was partly offset by treasury losses of Rs12.8bn.
Ex - of listing gain RoA for H1 was <1% vs reported RoA of 1.14%.
Retail loan growth of 14.5% YoY continued to lag overall loan growth and segments other than gold remained weak.
Bank continues to maintain full year guidance of 14-15% loan growth, 1% RoA and >3% domestic NIM

Macquarie on SBI
O-P TP Rs 1220
2Q: Exceptional gains aid earnings, loan growth remains healthy
Margins resilient
Asset quality remains healthy, ECL impact manageable
At 1.3x FY28E P/BV, valuations look comfortable against expected ROA above 1%.

CLSA on SBI
O-P, TP Rs 1325
Delivered a 2% NII beat versus our estimates, driven by an 11bp QoQ domestic NIM expansion.
Lower fee income and treasury losses led to a 3% PBT miss.
Domestic loans growth, at 17% YoY, was broad-based, while international loans declined 3% QoQ, adjusted for FCNR deposit-backed loans.
Deposit growth was healthy at 12% YoY, with 8% YoY CASA growth only soft spot.
In line with sector, asset quality continued to improve, with net slippages down 10bp YoY, even off a low base.
SBI should be largely unaffected by the new insurance distribution guidelines, with distribution income less than 3% of PBT.

Bernstein on SBI
Market Perform, TP Rs 1300
Headline earnings growth masked a softer underlying quarter, with lower credit costs & stake-sale gains supporting profitability.
Healthy loan growth & an 8 bps QoQ NIM recovery failed to lift underlying PPoP, which declined 1% YoY amid weaker other income and rising
expenses.
Excluding one-offs, EPS grew a more modest 5% YoY, while RoA declined 21 bps QoQ to 0.90%, compared with reported EPS growth of 13% and RoA of 1.19%

HSBC on SBI
Buy TP Rs 1220
2QFY27 underscored by strong NII / NIMs, while loan growth was lower, opex higher than estimates
Upgrade EPS by 4-8% for FY27-29e on stronger-than estimated NIM momentum and operating leverage playing out
TP cut as build in some discount for slower loan growth, lower multiples for some subsidiaries

CITI on SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1300
SBI's Rs230bn PAT (up 14% YoY) was lifted by a Rs72.9bn stake-sale gain, partly offset by a Rs12.8bn treasury loss and 15% YoY/38% QoQ opex growth.
NII rose 14% YoY/4.6% QoQ, beating estimates as NIMs expanded 8bps (vs our forecast of 2bps decline).
With 49% of loans linked external benchmarks (incl 32% repo-linked), NIMs should skew favorably in a rising-rate cycle, though management conservatively reiterated 3%+ NIM guidance. Loan growth was modest at 3.3% QoQ/18.2% YoY, lagging the system as corporate lending stayed flat.
Management retained 14-15% FY27 advances guidance, though we expect 16%+
Slippages stayed below 0.5%, credit costs under 0.35%.
ECL transition impact is pegged at Rs195bn (3.3% of net worth, 0.4% of advances).

Nomura on SBI
Neutral, TP Rs 1100
2QFY27 – NII beat, but loan growth slows
In-line core performance; weak treasury, higher opex offset by one time gain on SBI FUNDS stake sale
NIM expansion led to NII beat; higher opex, lower other income resulted in PPOP miss
Growth guidance maintained at 14-15% in FY27P; asset quality benign

Kotak Inst Eqt on SBI
Buy, TP Rs 1250
Reported 15% yoy earnings growth, led by a 7% yoy operating profit growth (stake sale in mutual fund). RoE at 15% was driven by healthy NII growth (~15% yoy), NIM recovering ~10bps qoq and a low credit cost (~30bps).
Asset quality remains a minor concern
Like franchise given its inexpensive valuation for a superior return profile.

items.description_html:
RT Marya Shakil
BIG CLARIFICATION BY THE ELECTION COMMISSION ON FORM 6 AND SIR

The ECI has clarified that voters whose names do not figure in the draft electoral rolls can submit Form 6 for fresh inclusion — even if they were enrolled previously.

Crucially, the Commission says:

• Previous enrolment does not make the Form 6 declaration false.
• No action under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, can be initiated merely because the elector was previously enrolled and has submitted Form 6.
• This protection applies provided the elector is not already enrolled in another Parliamentary or Assembly constituency and the declaration is otherwise lawful.

The clarification comes amid concerns among deleted voters that submitting Form 6 could expose them to prosecution for making a false declaration. The ECI has directed Chief Electoral Officers to publicise this clarification widely.

items.description_html:
Our latest report, "𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 - 𝗛𝟭 𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟳", examines the evolving fiscal landscape, revenue trends, expenditure pressures, and the outlook for government finances.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗶𝘀:

We expect the FY27 fiscal deficit to exceed the budgeted amount by Rs 0.7-0.8 trillion, leading to a fiscal deficit-to-GDP of 4.3-4.5%.

However, the Centre could meet its deficit target through the Rs 1 trillion Economic Stabilisation Fund.

Customs duties and GST collections are projected to remain supportive, with tax collections exceeding budget estimates in FY27.

However, we expect lower than budgeted revenues from excise duty collections and income taxes.

Overall, we expect gross tax revenue to see a shortfall of Rs 1 trillion in FY27.

Support from higher dividend transfers and disinvestments could contain the slippage in the overall receipts to Rs 0.5 trillion.

On the spending front, we expect the subsidy burden to rise by Rs 1.2 trillion, which could be partially offset by some revenue rationalisation and marginally lower capex.

Overall, we expect the total expenditure to exceed the budgeted target by Rs 0.3 trillion.

items.description_html:
Susan Electricals ~ Stronger H2 FY27 Ahead, Backed By ₹347 Cr Order Visibility

Susan Electricals' management expects a significantly stronger H2 FY27, supported by capacity expansion and growing demand for higher-value cables.

Key Management Takeaways:

• Order Visibility: ₹147 Cr confirmed order book and ₹200 Cr active pipeline, taking potential visibility to ₹347 Cr.

• CCV Line: Expected to become operational shortly, enabling participation in a wider range of HT cable projects.

• Cable Capacity: Expanding from 11,000 km to 16,000 km annually, a ~45% increase.

• Winding Wire Capacity: Increased from 3,307 to 4,200, with further expansion to 5,500 planned (~66% above the original capacity).

• Product Mix: Increasing focus on High-Tension (HT) cables and Medium Voltage Covered Conductors (MVCC).

• Balance Sheet: Operating cash flow has turned positive despite rapid business growth.

• Future Expansion: Company is in advanced stages of taking possession of newly acquired land for additional capacity.

The Bigger Picture: Susan Electricals is moving towards larger projects and higher-value products, with manufacturing expansion supporting its next phase of growth.

Key Monitorables: CCV commissioning, H2 order execution, margin recovery and conversion of the ₹200 Cr pipeline into firm orders.

items.title: Classic beginner-level flaw!! Good security by design systems use longer codes, rate limits for e.g. 3 attempts then lockout or cooldown, progressive ...
items.description_html:
Classic beginner-level flaw!! Good security by design systems use longer codes, rate limits for e.g. 3 attempts then lockout or cooldown, progressive delays, or CAPTCHA on failures.

A 4 digit OTP has only 10,000 probabilities and with no rate limit, anyone can break the code.

Bascially, encrypting a 4 digit code with a frontend public key and forgetting rate limits is a fundamental authentication design that should have never shipped. This is avoidable by design. All this is unbelievable.

Trust in technology is extremely hard to build but takes 1 reason to deminish that.


Neo: eMudhra login to download customer's certs can be cracked

Their 1FA login generates a OTP & sends it. It also sends a RSA public key to front end

They haven't rate limited checks, so you can offline brute force 0 to 9999 encrypted with public key & find the OTP

items.title: RT sphinx: My slightly contrarian, slightly in-agreement view is that India doesn’t have a Shenzhen. And without a dense manufacturing ecosystem, you...
items.description_html:
RT sphinx
My slightly contrarian, slightly in-agreement view is that India doesn’t have a Shenzhen. And without a dense manufacturing ecosystem, you won’t have the seeds of hard tech.

So debating vc investment is largely moot.

Indian hard tech startups are chasing high iq problems and that’s fine…but there’s still no Indian Anker. Even simple consumer electronics like battery chargers involve incredibly complex supply chains at cost. China has hundreds of Anker copycats operating at unit economics India simply cannot match. And that gap keeps widening as China pumps out more volume.

So founders naturally gravitate toward niche areas like rockets where the problem is more about engineering brilliance than supply chain economics. I understand the ambition, but very few startups can play that game.

Indian founders could build a saas ecosystem because it didn’t require govt support or a physical industrial base. Engineers, laptops, cloud infrastructure, and global distribution were enough. Startups could emerge first and the ecosystem followed.

Minimal govt interference - minimal infra dependency.

Hard tech works in reverse. You need suppliers, tooling, factories, skilled labor and volumes before startups can compete. These things take decades to compound, and VC money cannot shortcut that process.

In saas startups created the ecosystem. In hard tech, the ecosystem has to create the startups.

India needs a Shenzhen circa 2012 before it can have its Anker circa 2016.


Ashlee Vance: Why are Indian VCs so afraid to take risk and make money?

Someone should go to India and take risk and make money.

Our story - https://www.corememory.com/p/a-new-india-is-here

Meet SAGE, Spharaka’s own cybersecurity AI model.
Most AI in security today is a general-purpose model with a security prompt on top. It was trained on internet text, it looks at one alert at a time, and it can write a confident root cause that the evidence doesn’t support.

SAGE is built the other way round:
• Trained on 20 million real-world security events, not conversational data
• Built for security operations from first principles
• Reasons over tens of thousands of events per incident, across hosts, users and time
• Every conclusion grounded in verified telemetry and fully traceable

It is the intelligence core of Spharaka Sphere, built for SOCs handling 100,000+ alerts a day, with an average investigation time of 60 seconds per alert.

Generic AI summarises alerts. SAGE reasons over incidents.

Not a paid post, only supporting our own entrepreneurs build a reach.

items.title: I was sitting over coffee with a veteran wealth banker a few days back when he made a mild quip - "NSE listing will make half of private bankers joble...
items.description_html:
I was sitting over coffee with a veteran wealth banker a few days back when he made a mild quip - "NSE listing will make half of private bankers jobless."

As this enigma called NSE lists today after more than a decade of waiting, let me explain what he meant and why this matters. It won't be wrong to say that NSE pretty much created the pre-IPO investing category in India.

NSE has over 2.3 lakh private market shareholders. Another 70-80 lakh IPO applicants would be watching the tape at 10 am today with anticipation.

Interestingly, there were only 80 shareholders in 2016 when NSE first attempted to IPO. Even as recent as 2020, the count was a paltry 310 shareholders.

Almost an 800x surge post Covid!

Let us say NSE did to private markets what Jio did to data. And NSE was to private Wealth bankers what ULIP was to LIC agents :)

Suddenly, you did not need to be a PE fund in Singapore. Or on a VVIP list. You just needed a demat and a relationship manager who could whisper - “I can source a small lot.”

The Banker did not have to explain the company. The client already used it every trading day. Institutions sold, employees sold ESOPs, HNIs bought, then sold to the next HNIs. The round robin continued each year. Every transfer paid a spread - pocketing the Wealth house a sweet a 2-3% each time the stock changed hands. This is huge for an industry that makes just 30-40 bps on all Assets under Management.

As per UnlistedZone, NSE was half of all unlisted volume in India between 2023 and 2025!

The continued delay of a large, liquid, hot asset was the private bankers dream. It was demand-supply matched inventory.

Today that inventory lists - only on BSE, and not on its own boards. About ₹22,560 crore of pure Offer for Sale. The business doesn't need cash.

NSE created the pre-IPO market for likes of Tata Capital, SBI AMC, Swiggy, NSDL, Lenskart, etc. It created a category.

I don't think the veteran Banker was predicting pink slips. But I do think he was indicating the end of easy money for Wealth managers. The industry has turned a lot more competitive and the incentives are a lot more elusive + you hope for some luck. The money is now in the long run and business economics might have to readjust.

Wealth bankers will still do advice, credit, estate, "the ego massage" and the work of stopping a family from doing something stupid.

What ends today is the easy door-opener. For ten years NSE was that door. From today, it is a ticker.

#NSEIPO

items.description_html:
RT Tijori
Saudi Arabia is reducing oil cargoes to European refiners. Oil being cut off has happened to Europe before, Abqaiq (2019) and the 2022 Russia Disruption

At that time Indian refiners who benefitted massively were RIL, MRPL AND CPCL

RIL — the big direct winner. Most of what it makes is transport fuel, and the SEZ refinery is built to export.

MRPL — exports ~40% of its output, and half its slate is diesel + ATF. Exactly what Europe will be short of.

-CPCL is an indirect beneficiary. Products transferred from CPCL to parent IOCL are billed on an import-parity pricing (IPP) basis. When international product benchmarks and cracks increase, CPCL's realized refinery-gate prices rise immediately, boosting standalone GRM and operating cash flows.

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.title: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely...
items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.title: Given that oil price is the biggest impact India and many other countries are facing today because of the war, a coordinated effort to reduce fuel usa...
items.description_html: Given that oil price is the biggest impact India and many other countries  are facing today because of the war, a coordinated effort to reduce fuel usage may help reduce major impact. During COVID the world went into a complete shut down and oil prices had dropped to below $20 and futures had crashed to -$37 in April 2020. Maybe we can introduce partial work from home and keep industrial activities open, and I am sure this itself (if done globally) will help correct oil prices significantly. For India will help our trade deficit as well as lower pressure on our currency in addition to lowering input costs for many industries thereby reducing impact on profitability. COVID helped us develop and test technologies and platforms that made work from home easy and this may be a very good time to use them until war uncertainties remain. @narendramodi @nitin_gadkari @nsitharaman
